m.title: Insertion Sort · worked example
m.q: Trace insertion sort on [7,3,5,1,4], showing the sorted values after each insertion. [5 marks]
st: All five values begin in the unsorted array. The sorted array has five empty cells.
Take 7 from unsorted index 0. Keep the key separate until it is inserted.
Place 7 at sorted index 0. 1 value is now sorted.
Take 3 from unsorted index 1. Keep the key separate until it is inserted.
7 is greater than 3. Shift it right from sorted index 0 to 1.
Place 3 at sorted index 0. 2 values are now sorted.
Take 5 from unsorted index 2. Keep the key separate until it is inserted.
7 is greater than 5. Shift it right from sorted index 1 to 2.
Place 5 at sorted index 1. 3 values are now sorted.
Take 1 from unsorted index 3. Keep the key separate until it is inserted.
7 is greater than 1. Shift it right from sorted index 2 to 3.
5 is greater than 1. Shift it right from sorted index 1 to 2.
3 is greater than 1. Shift it right from sorted index 0 to 1.
Place 1 at sorted index 0. 4 values are now sorted.
Take 4 from unsorted index 4. Keep the key separate until it is inserted.
7 is greater than 4. Shift it right from sorted index 3 to 4.
5 is greater than 4. Shift it right from sorted index 2 to 3.
Place 4 at sorted index 2. The sorted array is complete; the unsorted array is empty.

k.q: Trace an insertion-sort comparison between two illustrative sound bit depths.
k.code:
previousDepth = 16
keyDepth = 8
if previousDepth > keyDepth then
    print("Shift previous right")
else
    print("Insert key here")
endif
p: Explain what sound bit depth measures and why more bits per sample increase raw data size.
k.a: 16 > 8, so Shift previous right. With keyDepth 24, Insert key here. Sound bit depth is the number of bits per sample; higher bit depth increases uncompressed file size for the same sample rate and duration. This represents an insertion decision, not the whole sort.
